name: Sechuran
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Extinct, 'poorly attested Peruvian language of uncertain affiliation' (Glottolog); only colonial wordlists (Martinez Companon) discussed in Urban 2019 — no stress data possible.

tone_statements.translation: ... they differ not only in the form of the language but in the accent; because, besides uttering the words in a tone like a sad chant, they swallow half of the final words, as if they lacked the breath to finish them. (Adams 1806: 'their enunciation, which is a kind of melancholy singing, they contract half of their last words, as if they lacked breath to pronounce them.')

V 'Sechura', section 'Sound system' pp. 104-108. p.104: Martinez Companon's (1782-90) Sechura list carries a grave accent on vowels (<tutù> 'water', <chùpchùp> 'star', <yòro> 'sun'); 'the significance of the grave remains unclear'; fn.103 argues against reading it as primary stress (double occurrence in <chùpchùp>, and <yòro> marked on the Spanish-default penult). p.107: Juan & Ulloa 1748 'acento.. como de canto triste' quoted; Urban says interpretations from pitch accent/tone to intonation are all possible and 'moot'. p.110: regional Spanish words of possible Sechura origin often end in…

tone.quote: There is an enigmatic statement concerning how the Sechura language sounded to the ears of a native speaker of Spanish by George Juan and Antonio de Ulloa … for besides their enunciation, which is a kind of melancholy singing, they contract half of their last words, as if they lacked breath to pronounce them. … I can think of several interpretations of this statement, ranging from pitch accent or tone, suggested by the “melancholy singing”, via voiceless vowels in word-final position to larger intonation patterns … But such speculations on phonetic details are moot
tone.locator: p. 107, ch. V Sechura, 'Sound system' (Spanish original of the 1748 remark in fn. 106, after Cerrón-Palomino 2004a: 89)
tone.says: Extinct, known only from colonial wordlists. A 1740s report that Sechura speech sounded like 'melancholy singing' could reflect tone, pitch accent or intonation; the source leaves it undecidable.

sources.citation: Urban, Matthias. 2015. El vocabulario sechurano de Richard Spruce. Lexis (PUCP) 39(2): 395-413.
sources.note: New transcription and facsimile of Spruce's 1864 Sechura wordlist (Kew). Discusses weakly articulated vowels (<kon'mpar> 'snake'; <cuctum> vs <cucatama> 'woman') and the Juan & Ulloa 'acento' remark; nothing on stress placement.

sources.locator: p. 16, Segunda parte, tomo III, Libro I, cap. I, par. 27 (= Engl. 1806 vol. II p. 13)
sources.note: The sole first-hand auditory remark on Sechura prosody. The Sechurans differ from other towns 'not only in the form of the language but in the accent', uttering their words 'en un tono, como de canto triste' (in a tone like a sad chant) and swallowing half of the final words as if out of breath. Impressionistic; Urban 2019: 107 lists possible readings (pitch accent or tone, devoiced final vowels, intonation contours with creaky/breathy or ingressive phonation) and calls them moot given the 43-word corpus. No tone inventory is recoverable; the grave accents in Martínez Compañón's Sechura list…
